metadata.title: Ultrametric Cantor sets and Growth of Measure

extraction_notes.note: Theorem 1 is argued in running text interrupted by Remarks 1 and 2; the argument is split into two proof parts around the remarks, the second with a uses edge to the first. The definition of primary/secondary scales inside the argument is kept as a step.

Theorem 2 only 'summarises' Section 4; the proof node starts at the paragraph applying the multiplicative model to a Cantor set, and the earlier derivation of the infinite-product solutions is kept as remarks.
remark or claim: the dimension log_3 2 and thickness 1 of the fluctuating s-sets are paper results but are argued and concluded inside one paragraph each with no separately stated claim.

The valuated exponent for s-sets is introduced inside a derived statement ('where rho ... is the valuated exponent'); split into a definition of v_R(x) and a claim carrying rho, proved by the following paragraphs.

Section 1.1 (Main Results) restates Theorems 1-3 and Proposition 2 in prose; no separate nodes were made for these previews. The 'regular metric' sentence of the introduction and the homogeneous/uniform terminology of Sec. 2 are not used later and got no node.
Solomyak's theorem on arithmetic sums of Cantor sets is only applied inside a sentence of the argument for Theorem 3, so it has no external node.
Equations (1) and (15) are the same scale invariant DE stated twice as numbered environments; both are emitted as environment facts, and (1) is left without edges.

nodes.statement: Notice that an infinitesimal gap of the form (0,epsilon ), epsilon rightarrow 0^+ is a segment of a line (i.e. an open interval) in the usual topology inherited from the real line. In the topology induced from the ultrametric mid cdot mid _u, the interval (0,epsilon ) instead is realized as a totally disconnected set and so itself is equivalent to a Cantor set tildeC. The structure of tildeC\ can, in general, be very arbitrary and even be independent of the original Cantor set C. In ref., we have, however, shown how this new ultrametric valuation for relative infinitesimals can lead to a topology identical to that of the original Cantor set C. In the following we give a brief out line of the procedure and also comment on the origin of the inequivalence of this ultrametric.

Notice that an infinitesimal gap of the form $(0,\epsilon ),$ $\epsilon
\rightarrow 0^{+}$ is a segment of a line (i.e. an open interval) in the
usual topology inherited from the real line. In the topology induced from
the ultrametric $\mid \cdot \mid _{u},$ the interval $(0,\epsilon )$ instead
is realized as a totally disconnected set and so itself is equivalent to a
Cantor set $\tilde{C}$. The structure of $\tilde{C}$\ can, in general, be
very arbitrary and even be independent of the original Cantor set $C$. In
ref.\cite {sd1, sd2}, we have, however, shown how this new ultrametric
valuation for relative infinitesimals can lead to a topology identical to
that of the original Cantor set $C$. In the following we give a
brief out line of the procedure and also comment on the origin of the
inequivalence of this ultrametric.

nodes.statement: 1. Middle third Cantor sets: As an application of the renormalised valuated exponent, let us first consider a class of s- sets where s=log_3 2, constructed as a slight variation of the process of Example 2, Sec.2. Let I=[0,1]. Also let 0<<delta_n=3^-(n+1)alpha_n lessapprox 1, \ n,=1,2,cdots (so that delta_n^-1gtrapprox 1), be a non-increasing sequence. For definiteness, one may choose alpha_n= q^-n, for a sufficiently large positive integer n and q>1. In that case alpha_n may be considered to belong to the range set of an appropriate Cantor function. Delete the middle open interval of length 1/3. Next, delete a length 3^(-2(1+alpha_1)) from each of the two closed subintervals. Then, delete the length 3^(-3(1-alpha_2)) from each of 2^2 closed subintervals. Call these two operations together O_1. O_n consists of two steps: deletion of 2^n+1 open intervals of length 3^-(n+1)(1+alpha_n), which is succeeded by the next deletion of lengths 3^-(n+2)(1-alpha_n+1) from 2^n+2 remaining closed subintervals. Notice that we are considering a set of fluctuating scale factors, i.e., in the (n+1)th step open intervals of slightly smaller sizes compared to the middle third set are removed. In the next step, however, open intervals of slightly bigger sizes are removed. As a consequence, we get a family of limit sets which are indistinguishable and equivalent to the middle third Cantor set at the level of the Hausdorff dimension, but nevertheless, distinguishable at the level of renormalised valuated exponents. Indeed, the total length of deleted open intervals viz., frac13+frac23^2delta_1+ frac2^23^3delta^-1_2 +cdots= 1+sum u_n equals 1, when the series of real numbers sum u_n vanishes. The sequence u_n is determined by the sequence alpha_n, i.e., alpha_n=log_3^(n+1) (1-frac3^(n+1)2^n tilde u_n)^-1 and alpha_n+1 =log_3^(n+2) (1+frac3^(n+2)2^n+1 tilde u_n+1) so that u_n=-tilde u_n, \ u_n+1=tilde u_n+1. Clearly, such a series exists. Hence, all such sets are of measure zero.

Since, sets with infinite Hausdorff dimension s=infty are excluded, by definition, rho indeed is positive rho>0.

nodes.raw_latex: {\bf 2. 1-sets:}  Irregular 1-sets \cite{falc}  are positive measure Cantor sets and are generally classified on the basis of fatness and/or uncertainty exponents. The LC renormalised valuation (\ref{eq32}) and (\ref{eq33}) now tells that $v_R(\tilde x)$ is a Cantor function corresponding to a subdominant residual Cantor set $C_s$, and so has the form $v_R(\tilde x)= \alpha _{i}\beta ^{m_{n}\rho}$.  As for the $s$-sets, the valuated exponent $\rho >0$ equals the inverse of the Hausdorff dimension of the residual set $C_s$. Consequently, $0< \rho\leq\infty$.
